ai-at-work.title: ‘What a joke’: Github Copilot’s new token-based billing spurs consternation among devs
ai-at-work.excerpt: The golden age of Microsoft's Github Copilot appears to be at an end.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: GitHub Copilot is moving from a flat monthly fee to a token-based consumption model, which means developers will pay based on actual usage rather than a fixed subscription. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals how AI tooling costs will increasingly work going forward, forcing you to think harder about governance, usage tracking, and budgeting for these "productivity" tools. The real joke isn't the pricing model itself, it's that companies spent two years telling people AI was free and unlimited, and now devs are surprised there's actually a meter running.

ai-at-work.title: I put Google’s 24/7 AI assistant Gemini Spark to work, and it’s actually pretty useful
ai-at-work.excerpt: Gemini Spark helps automate everyday tasks, from inbox summaries to local event planning, but it’s unclear why Google made it a separate product.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google launched Gemini Spark as a dedicated AI assistant aimed at automating routine workplace tasks like email summaries and scheduling, though the product strategy remains murky. This matters because your teams are already drowning in notification noise, and if an AI tool can actually reduce that friction without adding another login, it's worth evaluating. The real question isn't whether Spark works, it's whether your organization needs yet another Google product when you're probably already managing Gmail, Calendar, and Meet fatigue.

ai-at-work.title: As the browser wars heat up, here are the hottest alternatives to Chrome and Safari in 2026
ai-at-work.excerpt: We’ve compiled an overview of some of the top alternative browsers available today aiming to challenge Chrome and Safari.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: TechCrunch rounded up alternative browsers that are trying to chip away at Chrome and Safari's market dominance. This matters because your browser choice affects everything from security posture to how well your web apps perform across your workforce, and IT leaders need to actually understand what's out there beyond the default options. Here's the thing though: most organizations will stick with Chrome or Safari anyway because switching browsers organization-wide is like trying to herd cats with a laser pointer, so unless an alternative offers genuinely compelling security or performance gains, this is mostly interesting reading for the technically curious.

ai-at-work.title: Personal agents light the fuse as Snowflake and Databricks move up the AI stack
ai-at-work.excerpt: The artificial intelligence wave is starting to look a bit like the personal computer era – with some obvious differences. The first similarity is personal productivity. Individuals are taking control
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Snowflake and Databricks are moving beyond pure data infrastructure to build AI agents that let individual workers automate their own tasks without waiting for IT to build solutions. This matters because it shifts control of automation from centralized teams to end users, which means your workplace will suddenly have dozens of AI workflows running that nobody officially approved. It's the spreadsheet shadow IT problem all over again, except this time it's actually useful and potentially more dangerous if nobody's watching what data these agents are touching.

tools-tech.title: How to protect Windows 10 and 11 PCs from ransomware
tools-tech.excerpt: CryptoLocker. WannaCry. DarkSide. Conti. MedusaLocker. Qilin. The ransomware threat has exploded over the past decade, and it isn’t going away anytime soon; the news brings constant reports of new wav
tools-tech.dwp_take: Ransomware attacks keep getting more sophisticated and financially motivated, making Windows endpoints prime targets for criminals looking for quick paydays. Digital workplace professionals need to treat ransomware defense as a core operational requirement, not a checkbox on a security audit, because one successful attack can paralyze your entire organization's productivity. Here's the truth: most ransomware succeeds not because of some zero-day vulnerability but because someone skipped the backup, didn't patch their system, or clicked something they shouldn't have, which means your best defense is still the boring stuff done consistently.

digital-culture.title: The hidden gap between how others see you and what you’re worth
digital-culture.excerpt: The biggest career risk right now isn’t being replaced by AI. It’s being misunderstood by humans. A senior partner at a global consulting firm recently described to me what she thought she was experie
digital-culture.dwp_take: A consulting partner with serious accomplishments felt like a fraud because her organization didn't actually understand what she'd done or why it mattered. This matters to digital workplace pros because the same visibility gap happens constantly in remote and hybrid setups where your work happens off-camera and gets lost in async messages nobody reads. The real imposter syndrome isn't in your head; it's in your company's inability to see what you're actually contributing, which is why documenting wins and over-communicating impact has become a survival skill, not a personality flaw.

digital-culture.title: Behind the rise of the chief productivity officer and what it means for companies and employees
digital-culture.excerpt: Some employers are replacing HR directors with chief productivity officers to better align people, tech and business outcomes.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are creating chief productivity officer roles to replace traditional HR directors, betting that this role can better connect people strategy with technology and business results. This matters because it signals a fundamental shift in how organizations think about the employee experience: productivity is now seen as a boardroom priority rather than just an HR checkbox. Honestly, this feels like we're finally admitting that HR alone can't solve the people-technology gap, though I'd argue the real question is whether one person can either, or whether we just need HR and IT to finally stop sitting in separate cafeterias.

digital-culture.title: Hiring program in energy tech sector enlists military veterans to fill data center skills gap
digital-culture.excerpt: With an unprecedented surge in demand for skilled technicians, Schneider Electric eyes talent with military experience.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Schneider Electric is actively recruiting military veterans to fill data center technician roles as demand for skilled workers outpaces supply in the energy tech sector. This matters to digital workplace pros because data center operations are foundational to everything we do, and talent shortages directly impact infrastructure reliability and workplace continuity. Here's the thing though: if we're only now mining military talent pools to solve skills gaps, we've been sleeping on talent development for way too long, and this should be a wake-up call for broader workforce planning across the entire industry.

digital-culture.title: ‘We’re Just Getting the Crumbs Here’: Contractors Protest Layoffs at Meta’s European Headquarters
digital-culture.excerpt: Soon-to-be-laid-off Meta contractors say they’re being treated differently than Mark Zuckerberg’s full-time employees, who stand to receive more generous severance packages.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Meta contractors in Europe are getting substantially smaller severance packages than full-time employees during recent layoffs, creating a two-tier system that's left contractors feeling like second-class workers. This matters because it exposes the real gap between how companies treat permanent staff versus contingent workers, something that affects everything from morale to your ability to retain institutional knowledge across your digital workplace. Nothing says "we value our people" quite like paying some folks based on a different rulebook when the pink slips come around.

industry-news.title: 10 AI Prompting Tips That Improve ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Results
industry-news.excerpt: Improve AI chatbot results with 10 practical prompting tips for ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, from clearer context to better formatting. The post 10 AI Prompting Tips That Improve ChatGPT, Claude, and
industry-news.dwp_take: TechRepublic published a straightforward guide on how to get better outputs from the three major AI chatbots by using smarter prompting techniques like providing clearer context and better formatting. This matters because most of your workforce is already using these tools, and they're probably doing it badly, which means you're leaving performance on the table. Here's the thing: teaching people to prompt effectively costs nothing and beats buying another tool, so maybe do that first before your CEO asks why you need another AI platform.

industry-news.title: AI Upheaval, Security Warnings, and Legal Battles Define This Week in Tech
industry-news.excerpt: See what you missed in Daily Tech Insider from May 26–29. The post AI Upheaval, Security Warnings, and Legal Battles Define This Week in Tech appeared first on TechRepublic.
industry-news.dwp_take: This week brought the usual chaos: AI drama, security scares, and lawyers getting involved because apparently tech can't have nice things. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention because every one of these issues lands on their desk eventually, whether it's a new AI tool someone wants to deploy, a vulnerability the CEO read about on Twitter, or legal compliance questions nobody has answers for yet. The real fun starts when your CFO asks if you've "secured the AI" and you have to explain that securing AI is like securing water.

industry-news.title: Dell raises annual forecasts as AI boom continues to reward hardware vendors
industry-news.excerpt: Supply chain adjustments and shrewd management of the memory chip shortage help Dell capitalize on increased demand for AI
industry-news.dwp_take: Dell raised its annual financial forecasts because AI demand is driving hardware sales and their supply chain management is finally working in their favor. This matters because it signals that organizations are actually buying the infrastructure to support AI projects, which means your digital workplace strategies need to account for real hardware refresh cycles and the accompanying support costs. The funny part is that Dell's success here basically comes down to "we managed our supply chain competently," which shouldn't be remarkable, but in tech it apparently is.

industry-news.title: Post-cloud strategy: what comes after hyperscale?
industry-news.excerpt: Rising geopolitical risks and data sovereignty laws are driving enterprises toward regional clouds and hybrid infrastructure strategies
industry-news.dwp_take: Enterprises are moving away from the pure hyperscale cloud model toward regional and hybrid setups because of geopolitical tensions and tightening data sovereignty regulations. This matters to digital workplace leaders because your infrastructure decisions now directly impact compliance, user experience, and cost, which means you can't just hand everything to AWS and call it a day anymore. The irony is that after two decades of "move everything to the cloud," we're circling back to distributed systems that look suspiciously like what we had in 2005, except now it costs more and requires better governance.
